This is just a consequence of not warming up long enough.  The dual averaging
is optimizing too strongly in the tail yielding a shorter step size than is necessary
in the bulk.  This can be remedied by tweaking the warmup adaptation window
sizes or the dual averaging parameters but it’s really hard to select something
that works better as a default.  If you warmup for longer you should see everything
converge to 0.8.

I think it's a tradeoff here.  Adapting accept rate perfectly isn't
something we care about directly --- if the accept rate's too high,
then it's a bit ineffcient, but won't be wrong.  And the question is

Yet another research project for someone to do some evals on :-)

It's not much closer to the target of 0.8 with 10000 iterations and half warmup (see below).

Multiplying the number of iterations by 5 in order to get twice as many effective samples is not going to improve n_eff / second. But I continue to think that trying to make the defaults maximize n_eff / second for the largest class of models is not what defaults should be trying to accomplish. They should try to maximize the minimum n_eff / second over a wide class of models and I don't know if having an realized acceptance rate so close to 1 accomplishes that. More worrying, we have a few acceptance rates that are essentially zero, which is the sort of disaster that default arguments should be trying to prevent.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] acceptance rates vs. target
parts:
We need to separate out a few issues.

Firstly, the adaptation works fine one models we know HMC should fit, with the target
value of 0.8 quickly achieved.

Secondly, we can’t expect that success to carry over to all of the BUGS models, most
of which break every MCMC algorithm out there. With the nominal parameterizations
none of these are going to be geometrically ergodic and adaptation will be brittle as
a consequence. For example, step sizes that yield an average acceptance probability
of 0.8 in the bulk may cause way too many divergences in the tail (which we treat as
rejections, and hence skew the acceptance probability). The flip size are cases
where adaptation goes crazy during warmup (as is common without geometric
ergodicity) and the acceptance probability vanishes.

Before worrying about the adaptation we have to worry about the well-posedness
of all of these models. They need to be reparameterized and checked for heavy
tails (a la the HMC for hierarchical models paper). Once we know they fit then
we can see if the adaptation is still causing problems.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] acceptance rates vs. target
parts: > Now I'm worried (and maybe I should've been all along).

Most people don’t take geometric ergodicity seriously, but it’s
a big deal in practice and manifests as all of these pathologies
we keep seeing when people take careful looks at their models.

> I think this means we need to radically rethink our manual.
> We do not want to be providing example models (translations of
> BUGS models or otherwise), which should not be used.

I agree — but it’s hard to abandon them completely. Will users
be content when we say “BUGS/JAGS has never been fitting these
well, you just never had the diagnostics to see it”? Or, “we’ve
rewritten these examples so only compare these and ignore all
of the others”?

> And when you say won't fit, what's going to go wrong in terms
> of sampling? Are we not going to be sampling from the posterior or
> is it going to be so slow that the effect is the same?

It depends on your perspective. These algorithms are all ergodic,
just not geometrically ergodic. Technically this means that they will
eventually explore the entire posterior BUT we no longer have the
Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem so the accuracy of the Monte
Carlo estimates is unknown. For example, biases estimates
of hyperparameter means, as we see in hierarchical models.

Well, it would help if you understood how adaptation works.

As in documented in the manual, adaptation proceeds in three stages: an initial window where the metric is not updated, an intermediate window where the metric and step size are updated together, and a terminal window where the metric is set and the step size is given some time to find a good value conditioned on the final metric.  What's happening here is that for a simple model the terminal window is too small to compute a reasonable estimate of the average acceptance probability.  In particular, the estimated average is biased towards initial values and smaller acceptance probabilities (both because of who the Nesterov dual averaging works and because the distribution of acceptance probabilities is highly skewed) which is why the final step size is too conservative.

There are two simple fixes for a simple model: either increase the terminal window with adapt term_buffer=100 (the default is 75) or mess around with the dual averaging parameters.  One way to deemphasize the early values, for example, is to increase the gamma parameter with adapt gamma=0.15.  Both of these work for the Gaussian case, but without having an ensemble of models I'm not going to advocate changing any of the defaults.  We're on the safe side right now.
